lead: Today our calendar remembers Mar Sheelas, the Silas of the Acts of the Apostles, a trusted companion of Paul. The two readings fit his memory well. In the Epistle Paul says that no Christian lives or dies for himself or herself alone: “whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s.” In the Gospel Jesus looks at the crowds with compassion, “like sheep without a shepherd”, and asks his disciples to pray for labourers. Silas was one of those labourers, and he was answered in his own life. The key words are belonging and harvest.

set: Paul wrote to the Christians of Rome from Corinth, around AD 57. In chapters 14 and 15 he speaks to a quarrel in the Roman community. Some believers (Paul calls them “the strong”) felt at liberty to eat anything and did not keep special days; others (“the weak”) ate only vegetables and kept certain days as holy (14:1–6). Each side was tempted to look down on the other. Paul does not say who is right on every point. He asks both sides to remember who they belong to.
Our verses give the reason. Whatever we do, we do for the Lord, because he is Lord of the living and the dead.
str: vv. 7–8: no one lives or dies for himself or herself; living or dying, we are the Lord’s.
v. 9: this is why Christ died and lived again: to be Lord of the dead and the living.
v. 10: so why judge or despise a brother or sister? All will stand before God.
vv. 11–12: a word of Scripture: every knee will bow and every tongue give praise to God; each of us will be accountable to God.
¶ Paul moves from belonging, to the Lord’s death and resurrection, to the call for gentleness among believers.
kw: Paul uses this word again and again in these verses. In verse 11 he quotes Isaiah 45:23, where the speaker is the Lord, the God of Israel, and he applies the promise to Christ, as he does in Philippians 2:10–11.

The main verb of chapter 14 (see vv. 3, 4, 5, 10, 13). Paul does not forbid every kind of judging; he forbids despising a brother or sister over matters on which believers may differ in good conscience.
A raised platform from which a magistrate gave his verdict. Paul himself was brought before the bēma of the governor Gallio at Corinth (Acts 18:12–17), the city from which he writes.
vv: We do not live to ourselves, and we do not die to ourselves.
The Christian is not a private owner of his or her life. The sentence is not a burden but a comfort: our life and our death both have a meaning outside ourselves.
whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s.
This is one of the shortest summaries of Christian life in the New Testament. Nothing, not even death, takes us out of his hands.
For to this end Christ died and lived again, so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living.
The cross and the resurrection are the ground of the Lordship of Christ. Because he has passed through death, no one who has died is beyond his care.
For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God.

Some later manuscripts read “of Christ” here, borrowing the words of 2 Corinthians 5:10. The NRSV and the POC follow the oldest reading, “of God”. The meaning is the same in the end, since the Father judges through the Son (John 5:22).
every knee shall bow to me

Paul takes the words from Isaiah 45:23, which the Greek Old Testament renders with “every tongue shall confess”. The prophet pictures the nations turning to the one God; Paul reminds us that this same God is the judge of all, so no believer is the judge of another.
ch: The Catechism uses verse 9 when it speaks of the Lordship of Christ: Christ died and rose “that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living” (Romans 14:9), and so his Lordship reaches the whole of history and the world of the dead (CCC 668). The Church also teaches that full right to pass final judgment on the works and hearts of men belongs to Christ as Redeemer of the world (CCC 679). That is why Paul’s lesson is humble: the judge is already chosen, and it is not we. In the Roman funeral lectionary these verses are among the readings offered, because they tell the mourning that the dead are still “the Lord’s”. We pray in the Holy Qurbono for the living and the dead for the same reason: they belong to him, and we belong to one another in him.

set: These verses close the first great section of Matthew’s Gospel. In chapters 5–7 Jesus teaches (the Sermon on the Mount); in chapters 8–9 he heals and forgives. Matthew now sums up both in a single sentence, almost word for word like the summary in 4:23, so that the two chapters are enclosed between matching verses: “teaching … proclaiming … curing”.

Then he lets us see Jesus’ heart. The crowds are not a problem to be managed; they are scattered people to be gathered. The next verse, 10:1, begins the sending of the Twelve, so the prayer of 9:38 is answered at once by the people who are asked to pray.
str: v. 35: Jesus in all the towns and villages: teaching, proclaiming, healing.
v. 36: his compassion for the crowds, harassed and helpless like sheep without a shepherd.
vv. 37–38: the harvest is great, the labourers few: pray to the Lord of the harvest.
kw: From splanchna, the inner organs, the “gut” where deep feeling is felt. The word is used in the Gospels almost only of Jesus, or of figures in his parables who show God’s mercy. It is a love that moves a person to act.

In the Old Testament the Lord is the shepherd of Israel (Psalm 23; Ezekiel 34), and the leaders who fail the people are blamed as bad shepherds. Jesus sees the people as the flock that God himself promised to gather.
The verb literally means “to cast out, to thrust out”, and it is the same one used for driving out demons. The strong verb stresses how urgent the harvest is.
vv: Then Jesus went about all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, and proclaiming the good news of the kingdom, and curing every disease and every sickness.
Jesus goes to the people where they are. His teaching and his healing belong together: word and deed show the same kingdom.
When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.

The picture comes from Numbers 27:17, where Moses asks that the community not be “like sheep without a shepherd”, and God gives him Joshua, whose name in Hebrew is the same as Jesus. Jesus is the shepherd for whom Moses prayed.
The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few;
Jesus does not say that the field is poor. The need is large, and God’s work is ready; what is lacking is the hands.
therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.
The harvest belongs to God, and so does the sending. Prayer is the first work of everyone who cares for the Church’s mission. And those who pray find that they are sometimes the answer.
ch: The Church has always taken verse 38 as the command to pray for vocations: priests, deacons, monks and nuns, catechists and missionaries, and the faithful who serve in the world. The Catechism teaches that all the baptized share in Christ’s mission as priest, prophet and king (CCC 783–786), so “laborers” include every disciple, each in his or her own way. Mar Sheelas, whom we remember today, shows what this means. He was one of the leaders chosen by the apostles and elders at Jerusalem to carry their letter to Antioch (Acts 15:22), and he went with Paul on his second journey. At Philippi, in prison with Paul at midnight, he was heard “praying and singing hymns to God” (Acts 16:25). He prayed for the harvest, and then he went into it.

qa: Paul says “do not judge”. Does that mean Christians may never say that something is wrong?

No. In the same letter Paul speaks plainly of sin, and in 1 Corinthians 5–6 he asks the community to correct grave wrongdoing. What he rules out here is contempt: looking down on a brother or sister over matters on which believers may differ in good conscience, such as foods or customs. The final judgment of a person’s heart belongs to God alone (CCC 679). To tell the truth about good and evil, with love, is not the same as despising a person.
study: Paul says that we are the Lord’s in life and in death. How would this change one worry that I carry today?

Jesus sees the crowd and feels compassion before he gives any instruction. How can I look at the people around me, at home and in the parish, in the same way? Whom shall I pray for by name today, as a labourer for the harvest?
